source.title: Rethinking Parameter Counting in Deep Models: Effective Dimensionality Revisited
source.authors: Wesley J. Maddox; Gregory W. Benton; A. Wilson

record.tranche_reason: The paper says it follows Nakkiran et al.'s experimental setup and reproduces their ResNet18 width-sweep double-descent curve, while also testing related curves in other models.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own model-size, depth, and label-corruption results, plus reported effective-dimensionality/generalization comparisons. Cited results from other work are not recorded. Epoch-wise test-error behavior and test error as a function of training-sample count are not tested.
record.test_reason: The study follows Nakkiran et al.'s ResNet18 width-sweep setup on CIFAR-100, clean and with 20% label noise. It also runs linear-feature, two-spirals depth/width and CNN width-depth sweeps. It reports test loss and error curves and whether Hessian effective dimensionality tracks them. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue parameter counting is a poor complexity proxy. Hessian effective dimensionality, computed from training data, tracks generalization among models with comparable (near-zero) training loss, and explains double descent and width-depth tradeoffs. They call double descent 'an artifact of overfitting'. They note test-error double descent on CIFAR-100 appears only with label corruption.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows Nakkiran et al.'s ResNet18 width-sweep setup and reports reproducing its double-descent behavior. It additionally measures Hessian-based effective dimensionality and examines label corruption, linear models, and width-depth tradeoffs.
record.method_sensitivity: Test-error double descent differs between the clean and 20% label-corrupted ResNet18 conditions. In the two-spirals experiments, the reported outcome also differs between varying depth and varying width.
record.problems: The paper states that deep-model effective-dimensionality estimates use only the leading 100 Hessian eigenvalues and may be biased because small eigenvalues are omitted. Several curve values are shown only in figures. Test-error double descent is not reported for the clean CIFAR-100 condition, and the two-spirals width sweep reports constant test performance after training loss reaches zero.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant reported results were omitted.

untested.parts: Test error over training epochs is not measured.
Test error vs. training-sample count near the interpolation threshold is not measured.
Peak location along epochs or sample count. Whether Neff predicts the peak's location (rather than correlating with the curve) is not tested.
Multiple or triple peaks, and removal of the peak by optimally tuned regularization (weight decay fixed at 1e-4). BMA eliminating double descent is only cited.

missing.what: Neff (and alternative measures) correlation with test loss, test error and generalization gap for ResNet18 under 20% label corruption. Neff: 0.8772 / 0.87608 / 0.8578; log path-norm higher.

Generalization gap plotted against effective dimensionality is near-linear for interpolating linear models. Authors say a similar trend holds for ResNets and CNNs. This re-expresses double descent as monotone in effective complexity.
Comparison of Neff with PAC-Bayes, magnitude-aware PAC-Bayes, path-norm and log path-norm along the double-descent sweeps. Log path-norm reaches 0.9846 vs test error for ResNet18.
PAC-Bayes bounds spike near width 20, where training loss first reaches zero, in both clean and corrupted CIFAR-100.

record.verdict_notes: Table values in r10–r13 appear swapped between Tables 1 and 2: the extracted text places each caption below its block. ResNet18: 0.9434 loss, 0.9188 error, 0.9429 gap. CNN: 0.9305 loss, 0.9461 error, 0.9060 gap. The paper's claim that Neff beats other measures is not fully borne out by its own tables, where log path-norm is often higher. Neff uses only the top 100 Lanczos eigenvalues for deep models, and the authors acknowledge this biases the estimate. The record's V6 limits_scope on r2 was a misreading: clean-condition absence fits V6.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests test error across model width, including a label-corrupted condition; it does not test every deep-network architecture or setting.
Test error as a function of training epochs is not measured.
The paper varies data count in Bayesian examples but does not report test error as a function of training-sample count near an interpolation threshold.
The paper tests linear models and several neural-network settings, not all model classes.
Effective dimensionality is compared with generalization across width and depth; peak location over epochs and sample count is not tested.
The paper tests a 20% label-corruption condition. It does not test multiple or triple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The paper does not re-express the second descent as an ordinary U-shaped curve using an effective parameter count.
